Multinomial logit with random alternative-specific intercepts

Source: R/estimators.R
remnl.Rd

Fits the multinomial (or conditional) logit of mnl() with a normally distributed random intercept per unit in every non-base equation: a mixed logit whose only random coefficients are the constants, for panels and other grouped data where the cases of a unit share unobserved tastes for the alternatives.

Usage

remnl(
  formula,
  data,
  unit,
  nodes = 12L,
  id = NULL,
  alt = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"),
  cluster = NULL,
  nboot = 200L,
  cores = 1L,
  start = NULL,
  maxit = 1000L,
  reltol = 1e-10
)

Arguments

formula

A formula; see the section "Two data layouts" of mnl().

data

A data frame.

unit

Column name in data identifying the units whose cases share the random intercepts.

nodes

Gauss-Hermite points per dimension (default 12). Because the rule is adaptive its error does not grow with the number of cases per unit: against lme4::glmer(nAGQ = 25) at \(J = 2\) (150 units, 6 to 50 cases each, sd 1 or 2) 12 points put the log-likelihood within 1.2e-3 and the standard deviation within 0.01 percent, 8 points within 0.02 and 0.15 percent (verification/remnl_adaptive_check.R in the development repository). Raise it for large standard deviations with short panels. The analytic gradient is the quadrature of the exact gradient, which differs from the derivative of the quadrature likelihood by the quadrature error; with few nodes (6 or fewer), or large standard deviations and short panels, that difference can keep the optimizer from meeting its criterion (converged = FALSE with a small gradient), and more nodes cure it. The population-averaged probabilities of fitted() and predict(), an integral over the prior that no data narrow, use a finer rule: Gauss-Hermite with \(\max(\mathrm{nodes}, 10\sigma^2)\) points per dimension (rounded up to a power of two) while that is at most 128, and beyond that the trapezoidal rule with a step of at most \(1/\sigma\) standard deviations, whose size grows only linearly in \(\sigma\); both are accurate to about \(10^{-7}\) or better. The rule has at most 50000 points in all, or \(\mathrm{nodes}^{J-1}\) if that is larger, and at the cap the rule with the smaller error bound is used. The cap binds at \(J = 3\) for \(\sigma\) above about 7 (the error bound passes \(10^{-6}\) near 18), at \(J = 4\) above about 1.8 (bound above \(10^{-6}\) from 2.7), and at \(J \ge 5\) above about 0.9 (from about 1.6); the fit warns, with the bound and the number of points, whenever the bound exceeds \(10^{-6}\).

id, alt

For the long layout, the names of the case and alternative columns of data. Leave both NULL for the wide layout.

ref

The base (reference) alternative: a level of the response. Default: the first level.

weights

Optional frequency weights: a column name in data or a numeric vector with one entry per row (constant within a case in the long layout).

offset

Optional offset on the utility scale: in the long layout a column name or a vector with one entry per row; in the wide layout an \(n \times J\) matrix (columns in level order).

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (default), "opg", "robust" (over units, the observation of this likelihood), "cluster" (over clusters that nest the units), "bootstrap" (units resampled, a unit drawn twice counting as two units with their own intercepts; with frequency weights, multinomial unit counts), or "none".

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows, constant within a case); supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

nboot

Number of bootstrap refits for se = "bootstrap" (default 200).

cores

Number of parallel workers for the bootstrap (a PSOCK cluster; default 1). set.seed() before the call makes the resamples reproducible; serial and parallel runs use different random streams.

start

Optional starting values: the full parameter vector in the order of coef() but on the INTERNAL scale, which differs from coef() for the structural parameters (the logarithms of the inclusive values, scales, and standard deviations; the free Cholesky elements with a log diagonal for the multinomial probit covariance). object$theta of an earlier fit is on that scale. Rarely needed for mnl(), whose log-likelihood is globally concave; the other estimators start from the mnl() estimates (and imnl() from a multistart grid), so start serves to probe another basin of a non-concave likelihood.

maxit, reltol

Controls for the BFGS stage passed to stats::optim() (the plain mnl() is solved by damped Newton steps first, with BFGS as the fallback); the Newton polish that follows runs up to 25 further iterations with the analytic Hessian of the logit family or central differences of the analytic gradient otherwise.

Value

An object of class c("remnl", "choicemodel").

Details

$$V_{ij} = o_{ij} + x_i^\top \beta_j + w_{ij}^\top \gamma + u_{g(i) j}, \quad u_g \sim N(0, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_j^2)),$$ with \(u_{g b} = 0\) for the base alternative and independence across units and alternatives. With three or more alternatives the base defines the model, not only the labels. Intercepts independent relative to one base are correlated relative to another (\(u_j - u_c\) and \(u_k - u_c\) share \(u_c\)), which the diagonal model cannot represent. Fits with different ref are therefore different models, with different log-likelihoods and different tests against the multinomial logit. In the example below the log-likelihood is -488.49 with base a and -490.50 with base b (a fit whose standard deviation for a runs to zero, with a boundary warning), and the likelihood ratio against mnl() is 4.53 and 0.50. Choose the base before testing, on substantive grounds: the alternative whose utility is least expected to vary across units (an outside option, abstention). Fits with different bases have the same number of parameters and can be compared descriptively by their log-likelihoods, but a base chosen that way makes the test against the multinomial logit a maximum over the bases, for which the chi-square reference does not hold. The likelihood of unit \(g\) integrates the product of the MNL probabilities of its cases over \(u_g\) by adaptive product Gauss-Hermite quadrature (Liu and Pierce 1994; Pinheiro and Bates 1995): the nodes are centred at the mode of each unit's integrand and scaled by its curvature, with nodes points per dimension (\(J - 1\) dimensions, so \(\mathrm{nodes}^{J-1}\) points per unit; a warning above 20000 points). The standard deviations are reported as "sd:<alt>" (estimated on the log scale, delta-method standard errors). The observation is the unit: object$lli has one entry per unit, robust and outer-product standard errors are over units, cluster must nest units, frequency weights must be constant within a unit, and se = "bootstrap" resamples units. Fitted and predicted probabilities are population-averaged (integrated over the random intercepts). lr_test() against the mnl() fit of the same covariates tests \(\sigma = 0\), a boundary restriction whose chi-square p-value is conservative; vuong() against an MNL aggregates its contributions over units. At \(J = 2\) the model is the binomial generalized linear mixed model with a random intercept, and the fit matches lme4::glmer() with adaptive quadrature. Everything else is as in mnl(), except that there is no fe or bias_correct (the unit effects are the random intercepts) and that simulate() draws one intercept vector per unit and then the unit's cases given it, while fitted() and predict() are the population-averaged probabilities. The IIA tests and hl_test() refuse these fits (the cases of a unit are dependent). fit_stats() and the information criteria use the number of cases as \(n\).

References

Liu, Q. and Pierce, D.A. (1994). A note on Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Biometrika, 81(3), 624-629. doi:10.1093/biomet/81.3.624

Pinheiro, J.C. and Bates, D.M. (1995). Approximations to the log-likelihood function in the nonlinear mixed-effects model. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 4(1), 12-35. doi:10.1080/10618600.1995.10474663

See also

mnl(), nlogit(), hev(), mnprobit(), lr_test()

Other estimators: hev(), imnl(), mnl(), mnprobit(), nlogit(), rologit()

Examples

set.seed(1)
G <- 60; T <- 5; unit <- rep(seq_len(G), each = T)
x1 <- rnorm(G * T); u <- rnorm(G, 0, 1)
V <- cbind(0, 0.3 + 0.8 * x1 + u[unit], -0.2 - 0.6 * x1)
P <- exp(V) / rowSums(exp(V))
y <- apply(P, 1, function(p) sample.int(3, 1, prob = p))
d <- data.frame(y = factor(c("a", "b", "c")[y]), x1, unit = factor(unit))
m <- remnl(y ~ x1, data = d, unit = "unit", nodes = 8)
summary(m)
#> Multinomial logit with random alternative-specific intercepts (60 units, 8-point Gauss-Hermite per dimension) 
#> Call: remnl(formula = y ~ x1, data = d, unit = "unit", nodes = 8)
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)  0.56630    0.16204   3.495 0.000474 ***
#> b:x1           0.73601    0.18854   3.904 9.47e-05 ***
#> c:(Intercept) -0.07182    0.19165  -0.375 0.707834    
#> c:x1          -0.65526    0.20311  -3.226 0.001255 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Random alternative-specific intercepts: standard deviations (no z test: sd = 0 is on the boundary; use lr_test() against the mnl() fit):
#>      Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> sd:b   0.4065     0.3232      NA       NA
#> sd:c   0.3018     0.4706      NA       NA
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -282.432 on 6 parameters, 300 cases. AIC 576.86, BIC 599.09.
lr_test(mnl(y ~ x1, data = d), m)
#> The restriction sd = 0 is on the boundary of the parameter space: the chi-square p-value is conservative (the null distribution is a mixture of chi-squares with fewer degrees of freedom); boot_lr_test() gives a calibrated p-value.
#> Likelihood-ratio test
#>   LR = 0.8967 on 2 df, p = 0.6387
